title: Ordered Integer, Multiples, and Merge Streams
prompt:
Implement three classes using the supplied `Stream` interface. Calling `stream.next()` or Python's `next(stream)` consumes one value; `iter(stream)` returns the same stream. Exhausted finite streams keep raising `StopIteration`.

### Part 1 — Ordered integer stream

`OrderedIntStream(items)` yields a finite, nondecreasing list of integers in its given order, including duplicates. The caller will not modify `items` during iteration.

### Part 2 — Multiples stream

`MultiplesStream(base)`, for a positive integer `base`, yields `base, 2 * base, 3 * base, ...` indefinitely. Generate values as requested.

### Part 3 — Merge stream

`MergeStream(streams)` consumes distinct input `Stream` objects from their current positions and yields all their values in nondecreasing order. Inputs may be finite or infinite. Preserve every occurrence of equal values. Empty inputs are allowed; the merge is exhausted when every input is exhausted.

Consume incrementally: buffer at most one upcoming value per input, rather than materializing the inputs. With `k` inputs, use O(k) auxiliary space and O(log(k + 1)) work per returned value after initialization. Do not reset or recreate input streams.

| Stream | First values |
| --- | --- |
| `OrderedIntStream([-2, 1, 1])` | `-2, 1, 1`, then exhausted |
| `MultiplesStream(3)` | `3, 6, 9, ...` |
| Merge of `[1, 4]` and multiples of 3 | `1, 3, 4, 6, 9, ...` |

Follow-up: explain how you handle equal values and why the merge can produce a finite prefix even when an input is infinite.

example.input: s = MergeStream([OrderedIntStream([1, 4]), MultiplesStream(3)]); [s.next() for _ in range(7)]
example.reasoning: Consume only the requested prefix; the multiples stream has no end.
